video_caption: The video segment opens with a white background displaying the title "General wave properties" at the top left. Below it, two sentences read: "Waves transfer energy from one place to another." and "They all involve some kind of oscillation." Centered on the screen is an abstract image featuring numerous glowing, wavy orange lines intertwined against a dark background, some lines with brighter, almost sparkling points, visually representing energy or wave motion. A male voiceover explains that waves transfer energy and involve oscillation, using examples like sound waves and light waves. At 00:41, the screen transitions to a new slide titled "Wave motion experiments." This slide is divided into four sections, each with a label and an illustrative image: "Water ripples" shows a close-up of concentric circles spreading on a water surface; "Slinky" displays a colorful Slinky toy, stretched out and curved; "Light" is represented by a cartoon drawing of a yellow lightbulb emitting light rays; and "Rope" depicts a child holding one end of a wavy rope, with the other end tied to a green tree. The voiceover continues to describe these various wave motion experiments.

The video segment opens with the text "The wavefront" followed by "The wavefront is a line where the wave is in phase." below it. The background displays a still photograph of a harbor on a sunny day. The image shows a sandy and rocky beach in the foreground, leading to calm water where two concrete breakwaters form a narrow opening to the open sea. The sky is clear and blue. As the speaker explains the wavefront, a small red circle appears and moves along a white wave line within the harbor entrance, illustrating the concept of the wavefront. This red circle highlights different sections of the same wave as the explanation progresses, emphasizing that the wave is "in phase" along this line.

The video segment opens with a white background displaying the title "Wave speed" in black text, followed by the description "Wave speed is measurment of how fast a wave moves forward. Wave speed is measured in m/s." Below the text is an image of a military jet flying horizontally across a light blue sky with faint white clouds. The jet is surrounded by a large, opaque, white, oval-shaped vapor cone around its mid-section. During the narration, a red dot briefly appears on the jet's nose, then moves to the bottom and then the top of the vapor cone, highlighting different areas. The scene transitions to a different slide titled "Frequency" in black text, with the description "Frequency is the number of wave cycles per second. Frequency is measured in Hertz." Below this text is a close-up image of a person wearing a grey t-shirt and blue jeans, playing a blue electric guitar with a white pickguard. Their right hand strums the strings with a pick, while their left hand is on the fretboard.

The video opens with the word "Frequency" displayed at the top of the screen. Below it, a person's torso and arms are shown, focusing on their hands playing a blue electric guitar with a white pickguard. The person wears a light-colored shirt and jeans, with a bracelet on their left wrist and a ring on one finger of their left hand, which is positioned over the guitar's strings near the pickups. A red amplifier is partially visible in the background to the left. At the bottom of the screen, the text reads: "Frequency is the number of wave cycles per second. Frequency is measured in Hertz." The scene then transitions to new text, "Wavelength," at the top. Below this, more text explains: "Wavelength is the distance it takes for the wave to repeat its self - the length of one wave. Wavelength is measured in metres." Underneath this explanation, a diagram illustrates two waves: a solid blue wave and a dotted red wave, both oscillating around a horizontal line marked with black dots. Arrows labeled with the Greek letter lambda (λ) indicate the wavelength for each wave, showing the distance over which the wave pattern repeats.

The video segment displays a white background with the title "Wavelength" in the top left corner. Below it, text reads: "Wavelength is the distance it takes for the wave to repeat its self - the length of one wave. Wavelength is measured in metres." Below the text, a diagram shows two sinusoidal waves, one blue and one red, oscillating around a horizontal black line. Black dots are placed on the waves at various points, including peaks, troughs, and where they cross the horizontal line. A prominent blue double-headed arrow labeled "λ" (lambda) spans horizontally between two consecutive peaks of the blue wave, visually representing its wavelength. A smaller red double-headed arrow, also labeled "λ," indicates the wavelength of the red wave, stretching from one peak to the next. As the narrator speaks, a red dot appears and moves across the blue wave, first highlighting the distance between two successive peaks as one wavelength, then illustrating the distance from a starting point (where the wave crosses the horizontal line, moving upwards) to the next equivalent point, and finally appearing on a peak of the red wave to show its corresponding wavelength.

The video segment features a white background with black text at the top left corner that reads "Wavelength." Below this title, two sentences further explain the concept: "Wavelength is the distance it takes for the wave to repeat its self - the length of one wave. Wavelength is measured in metres." Below the text, an illustration depicts two sinusoidal waves: a blue wave with a larger amplitude and longer wavelength, and a red wave with a smaller amplitude and shorter wavelength, both superimposed on a central horizontal black line representing the rest position. Black solid circles mark the peaks, troughs, and zero-crossing points for both waves. A large blue double-headed arrow with the label "λ" (lambda) is positioned above the blue wave, illustrating its wavelength from peak to peak. A smaller red double-headed arrow, also labeled "λ," is located below the red wave, indicating its wavelength from trough to trough. Throughout the segment, a blinking red dot, similar to a laser pointer, appears and moves to highlight specific points: first on a trough of the red wave, then briefly on another trough of the red wave, and finally resting briefly on the blue "λ" label above the blue wave.

The video displays a white background with a yellow wavy line, representing a wave, centered on the screen. A straight black diagonal line runs through the middle of the wave, labeled "Amplitude" at the top left. Text below the wave reads: "The distance from the peak of the wave to the rest position is the waves apli-tude." (The word "aplitude" appears to be a typo and is meant to be "amplitude.") "Amplitude is measured in metres." An upward-pointing arrow labeled "a" shows the vertical distance from the black rest line to the first peak of the wave, indicating the amplitude. Another horizontal arrow labeled "b" spans the distance between two consecutive troughs of the wave, representing the wavelength. As the narrator speaks, a red dot highlights different points on the black rest line and then moves to the peak and trough of the wave, illustrating the concept of amplitude as the distance from the rest position to either the peak or the trough.

The video displays a white background with text in the upper left corner stating "The wave equation," followed by "Wavespeed = Frequency x Wavelength" in red. Below this, a large handwritten red equation, "V = f x λ," is centrally presented. As the video progresses, red handwritten annotations appear: an arrow points from 'V' with "m/s" (meters per second) indicating its unit; another arrow from 'f' shows "Hz or s⁻¹" (Hertz or per second) for frequency; and a third arrow from 'λ' points to "m" (meters) for wavelength. Around the 00:23 mark, a red handwritten triangle diagram appears in the bottom-left corner. The triangle is divided into three sections: 'V' at the top and 'f x λ' at the bottom, separated by a horizontal line. A small red dot then moves within this triangle to illustrate how to use it: first hovering over 'f x λ' to imply V = f x λ, then over 'f' to imply f = V/λ, and finally over 'λ' to imply λ = V/f.

The video opens with a white background displaying the text "Reflection" and "Reflection occurs when a wave meets a boundary." Below the text, a hand-drawn illustration depicts a stick figure person on a sandy shore next to blue water. The person has a speech bubble saying "Help!!", and concentric pink and blue wave-like arcs are shown emanating from them, moving across the water towards a gray cliff on the right, labeled "Cliff" with an arrow pointing to it. A red dot is animated to move along the path of the waves: first moving from the person towards the cliff, then disappearing briefly upon hitting the cliff, and reappearing to move back towards the person as a reflected wave. Above the water, between the person and the cliff, two horizontal arrows indicate the back and forth movement of the waves. The scene then transitions to a new white background with the text "Refraction" and "When waves travel from one material to another the wave speed can change. This causes refraction and the direction of the wave will change." Below this text, two images are displayed, tilted slightly to the right. The left image shows a yellow beam of light entering a rectangular glass block on a dark blue surface, bending as it passes through and exits the block. The right image displays a pattern of parallel, wavy black and white lines, which appear to change direction and spacing as if passing through a different medium, demonstrating wave refraction.

The video displays a static slide with the title "Refraction" and a description that reads: "When waves travel from one material to another the wave speed can change. This causes refraction and the direction of the wave will change." Below this text, two images are presented, both tilted slightly as if laid on a surface. The image on the left shows a clear, rectangular block, likely made of glass or plastic, resting on a dark teal background. A thin, bright yellow beam of light, originating from the bottom-left, enters the block at an angle, bends downwards as it passes through the block, and then bends back upwards upon exiting, continuing parallel to its original path but laterally displaced. A red animated dot moves along this light beam, illustrating its path of travel and refraction. The image on the right depicts a pattern of parallel grayscale bands, resembling waves, initially broad and angled from the top-left to the bottom-right. These waves encounter a diagonal boundary line, after which they become visibly narrower and change their angle, appearing to bend towards a more horizontal direction. A red animated dot traverses this image, moving along one of the wave crests from the top-left region, across the diagonal boundary, and continuing along the bent and narrower wave crest in the bottom-right, demonstrating the change in wavelength and direction as the wave enters a new medium.

The video segment displays a static white background with a tilted rectangular box in the center, containing an illustration of "Diffraction." At the top left of the screen, the word "Diffraction" is written in black text. Below it, the definition reads: "When a wave encounters a slit the wave will spread out - this effect is called diffraction." The illustration within the box compares two scenarios of waves passing through slits. On the left, parallel gray waves, indicated by red arrows moving right, approach a barrier with a relatively wide gap. After passing through this gap, the waves spread out slightly. On the right, the same type of parallel gray waves, also indicated by red arrows, approach a barrier with a much narrower gap. After passing through the narrower gap, these waves spread out significantly more, forming distinct semi-circular patterns, with red arrows showing their diverging paths.

The video displays a static image with text at the top and a diagram below. The text reads: "Diffraction" followed by "When a wave encounters a slit the wave will spread out - this effect is called diffraction." The diagram, set against a white background with a slightly tilted black border, illustrates the phenomenon of diffraction in two parts. On the left, parallel gray wavefronts move horizontally from left to right towards a barrier with a wide slit. After passing through this wide opening, the wavefronts continue mostly as parallel lines, with only slight bending or spreading at their edges. Red arrows indicate the direction of wave propagation. During the video, a small red circle briefly appears and moves along one of the wavefronts before the wide slit. On the right, the same parallel gray wavefronts approach a barrier with a much narrower slit. Upon passing through this narrow opening, the wavefronts noticeably spread out, forming clear semi-circular patterns, and red arrows depict this outward spreading of the wave.
